title: 2.4.15 Plain English to Pseudocode: continue Skips, Doesn't Leave
description: Turn plain-English steps into pseudocode for a loop that skips the even numbers: continue ends one round early but stays in the loop.
sourceRef: designed: charts Definition 2.4.3's figure (continue) for book 2.4.4, contrasted with the break chart in 2.4.11

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English:

**1.** For each `i` from `1` to `6`, do steps 2 to 4.

**2.** Check whether `i` is even (`i % 2` is `0`).

**3.** If it is even, **continue**: skip the rest of this round and go straight to the next `i`. You are still in the loop.

**4.** Otherwise (an odd `i`), print `i`.

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you read it: the diamond has two exits, and **both** go back to the hexagon. Compare that with a `break`, whose exit would go to the end of the program.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Number every line, including indented ones. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `FOR EACH n FROM 1 TO 9` ... `END FOR` (a loop, the steps inside indented)
- `IF n is 5` ... `END IF` (a check, the steps inside indented)
- `CONTINUE` (skip the rest of this round) and `BREAK` (leave the loop altogether)
- `PRINT n` (show something)

Plain English is fine. Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, trace it by hand: `i` = 1 prints, 2 is skipped, 3 prints, 4 is skipped, 5 prints, 6 is skipped. It should print `1`, `3`, `5`.
hints: continue is not break: the loop keeps going with the next i.
The print comes after the check, so it only happens when continue did not fire.

requirements.title: Numbered steps
requirements.description: Number your steps 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: Write at least four lines that start with a number, each with a step written after it.

requirements.title: The loop counts i from 1 to 6
requirements.description: A loop step that goes through i from 1 to 6.
requirements.hint: Add a loop step: for each i from 1 to 6.

requirements.title: The check is "is i even?"
requirements.description: Inside the loop, a check for whether i is even (i % 2 is 0).
requirements.hint: Add a check: is i even, meaning i % 2 is 0?

requirements.title: Even means continue (skip), not break
requirements.description: When i is even the steps CONTINUE: skip the rest of this round and move on to the next i. Not leave the loop.
requirements.hint: Under the even answer, write CONTINUE (skip to the next i). Do not leave the loop.

requirements.title: The print comes after the check
requirements.description: i is printed after the check, so only the rounds that did not continue print.
requirements.hint: Put the print after the END IF, so even numbers never reach it.

requirements.title: The print is inside the loop
requirements.description: The print is a step of the loop body: the loop ends after it, so the next i comes round again.
requirements.hint: Close the loop (END FOR) after the print, not before it.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The program is: for (let i = 1; i <= 6; i++) { if (i % 2 === 0) { continue; } console.log(i); }. It prints 1, 3, 5. The point: continue skips the rest of ONE round and goes on to the next i; it does not leave the loop (that would be break). Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, ELSE, END IF, FOR EACH, END FOR, CALL, PRINT, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite (for example the even case using break or leaving the loop, or the print placed before the check). Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: Numbered steps
rubric.description: The student numbered their steps (1. 2. 3. or similar), at least four of them.

rubric.title: The loop counts i from 1 to 6
rubric.description: A loop step that goes through i from 1 to 6.

rubric.title: The check is "is i even?"
rubric.description: Inside the loop there is a check for whether i is EVEN (i % 2 equals 0). A check for odd numbers, or a different divisor such as 3, does not meet this.

rubric.title: Even means continue (skip), not break
rubric.description: When i is even the steps CONTINUE or skip the rest of this round and go on to the next i, staying in the loop. If the even case BREAKS, stops or leaves the loop, this is NOT met.

rubric.title: The print comes after the check
rubric.description: The print of i comes AFTER the even check (after the continue/END IF), so even numbers never reach it. A print before the check would print every number.

rubric.title: The print is inside the loop
rubric.description: The print is INSIDE the loop (before the loop is closed), so it can run for each odd i. A print after the loop has ended runs only once.
